scenes.label: Meet the team
scenes.title: Space for every team
scenes.caption: A sports club marks activity zones on a courtyard grid. Each cell represents one square mat. A clear entrance lane must let visitors move between the gate and the far end.

scenes.label: The problem
scenes.title: Name a cell
scenes.caption: Rohan labels rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right, starting at one for people reading the board. Saying row two, column three now identifies exactly one cell, even when the paper is passed around.

scenes.label: How it works
scenes.title: Area and shape
scenes.caption: The first zone needs six mats arranged as two rows of three. A single strip of six also has area six, but it does not meet the shape requirement. Counting cells checks area; checking their arrangement tests shape.
scenes.dialogue: Equal counts can hide different shapes.

scenes.label: Your decision
scenes.title: Turn the zone
scenes.caption: Mina rotates the rectangle a quarter turn. It now uses three rows of two, while its area stays six. Choose the claim that survives this transformation. Rotation changes orientation, so the club must still check the nearby access lane.
scenes.dialogue: Same area does not promise a clear lane.

scenes.label: What changes
scenes.title: A reflected plan
scenes.caption: The team also tries a mirror image across a vertical centre line. Left and right positions swap, but rows stay unchanged. They compare labelled cells instead of turning the whole sheet upside down and accidentally changing both directions.

scenes.label: Enter the lab
scenes.title: A smaller boundary
scenes.caption: Rain closes one courtyard column. Your final challenge uses the remaining cells and a smaller zone. Build only the specified shape, then inspect every boundary and the protected lane. Save a checked layout rather than an attractive but untested sketch.
scenes.dialogue: The changed boundary needs a fresh check.
